title: Three Million New Spectra of the Sky
hook: SDSS-V has released over three million spectra and, for the first time, opened its optical survey to the Southern Hemisphere — turning a sky map into a time-lapse.
key_points: The release adds more than three million new optical spectra to the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's fifth generation.
It is the first time SDSS-V optical spectroscopy covers the Southern Hemisphere, extending the survey to the whole sky.
A spectrum splits an object's light by wavelength, revealing composition, temperature, motion, and distance — far more than an image alone.
The data include rare stars, glowing nebulae, hundreds of thousands of X-ray sources, and supermassive black holes.
Repeat observations track how those black holes change over time, making the survey a record of variability, not just a snapshot.
content_html: Most of what astronomers know about distant objects comes from spectra: split an object's light into its component wavelengths, and the pattern of lines tells you what it is made of, how hot it is, how fast it is moving, and — through redshift — how far away it sits. Images tell you where things are; spectra tell you what they are.
extra_html:
The Sloan Digital Sky Survey's fifth generation has released more than three million new spectra, and for the first time its optical observations extend into the Southern Hemisphere, giving the survey genuine all-sky reach. The catalogue spans rare stars, glowing nebulae, hundreds of thousands of X-ray sources, and large numbers of supermassive black holes.

The part that makes it more than a bigger catalogue is repetition. By revisiting targets, the survey records how objects change — particularly accreting black holes, whose brightness and spectral features vary as material falls in. That turns a map into something closer to a time-lapse of the sky. See ScienceDaily's report for the release details.

related.title: Catching Black Hole Pairs by Their Flicker
related.hook: Tightly bound supermassive black hole pairs are nearly invisible. A new idea: watch for stars that flash as the black holes' gravity bends and magnifies their light.

related.title: NASA's James Webb catches a supermassive black hole feeding
related.hook: JWST just captured a supermassive black hole's fuel supply in action: gas pouring into a fast-spinning disk, hinting these giants recycle their own fuel instead of just consuming and discarding it.

related.title: Black Holes
related.hook: A black hole is a place where gravity wins so completely that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the edge called the event horizon.

flashcards.prompt: What does a spectrum tell astronomers that an image cannot?
flashcards.back_html: Splitting light by wavelength reveals what an object is made of, how hot it is, how fast it is moving toward or away from us, and — through redshift — how far away it lies.

flashcards.prompt: Why does repeatedly observing the same objects matter for this survey?

choices.text: It captures how sources like supermassive black holes change over time
It is the only way to determine an object's chemical composition
It corrects for the Earth's rotation, which otherwise blurs the spectra

flashcards.explanation_html: Composition comes from a single spectrum. Repeat visits add the time axis, turning a static catalogue into a record of variability — essential for accreting black holes, which brighten and fade.
